chief_complaint: brief loss of consciousness, lucid interval, then severe headache
hpi_details: 22-year-old male was struck in the side of the head with a baseball bat. He lost consciousness for 2 minutes, then woke up and felt fine (lucid interval). Two hours later, he developed a severe headache, began vomiting, and is now rapidly becoming lethargic.
ideas: He thinks he has a severe sports concussion and a migraine triggered by being struck with the baseball bat.
concerns: He is worried that his skull is cracked and bleeding inside, which could cause permanent brain damage.
expectations: He hopes to receive an immediate emergency head scan and strong IV medication to halt the vomiting and head pain.

investigation_events.title: Emergency non-contrast head CT
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency CT result is now available. Airway management, temporizing herniation treatment, and operative preparation should not be delayed.

results.value: Large right temporal biconvex epidural hematoma with an overlying temporal bone fracture, 11 mm leftward midline shift, and early uncal herniation

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Epidural Hematoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Epidural Hematoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

This presentation is a time-critical traumatic brain injury: stabilize airway, breathing, circulation and cervical spine while arranging immediate neurosurgical involvement and non-contrast head CT when it does not delay life-saving intervention.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: brief loss of consciousness, lucid interval, then severe headache

Key HPI features: 22-year-old male was struck in the side of the head with a baseball bat. He lost consciousness for 2 minutes, then woke up and felt fine (lucid interval). Two hours later, he developed a severe headache, began vomiting, and is now rapidly becoming lethargic.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Epidural Hematoma.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Epidural Hematoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Subdural hematoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fixed dilated pupil.
management_principles: Treat as a surgical emergency: stabilize airway, breathing, circulation and cervical spine, with immediate neurosurgical consultation and non-contrast head CT if this does not delay intervention.

Urgently evacuate a confirmed epidural hematoma when indicated by imaging and neurologic status; use brief controlled hyperventilation only as a temporizing measure for clinical herniation while definitive care is arranged.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: brief loss of consciousness, lucid interval, then severe headache

22-year-old male was struck in the side of the head with a baseball bat. He lost consciousness for 2 minutes, then woke up and felt fine (lucid interval). Two hours later, he developed a severe headache, began vomiting, and is now rapidly becoming lethargic.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 55, BP 160/90 (Cushing's reflex indicating raised ICP). GCS is deteriorating (E2 V3 M4 = 9). Right pupil is dilated and sluggish to light. Left-sided hemiparesis noted.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Epidural Hematoma with impending uncal herniation.
reference_soap.plan: Surgical emergency. Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation and cervical spine; intubate for airway protection given deteriorating consciousness. Obtain immediate non-contrast head CT if it does not delay life-saving intervention and involve neurosurgery immediately. Evacuate an epidural hematoma urgently when indicated by imaging and neurologic status. Use brief controlled hyperventilation only as a temporizing measure for clinical herniation while definitive care is arranged.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Epidural Hematoma
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Epidural Hematoma
Initiate time-critical stabilization, imaging, and neurosurgical management for suspected epidural hematoma

teaching.one_liner: A ruptured middle meningeal artery after head trauma, with a brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval, then rapid deterioration.
red_flags: Fixed or dilated pupil, new unilateral weakness, or rapidly falling level of consciousness
Repeated vomiting, seizure, or signs of raised intracranial pressure after head injury

must_ask.say: Did you lose consciousness right after the injury?
Did you feel fine for a while afterward?
How has your headache changed since?
How did the head injury happen?

history.answer: I got hit in the side of the head with a baseball bat earlier today, and now I have an unbearable headache and feel like I'm passing out.
Right after getting hit I was knocked out, but after waking up I felt fine for about two hours. Then this terrible headache came on rapidly over about fifteen minutes.
The severe pain started about an hour ago and has been constant and worsening. I have never had a headache like this before in my life.
It's pounding on the right side of my head, right where the bat struck me near my temple.
It is an intense, throbbing pressure that feels like my skull is going to burst. I would rate it a ten out of ten.
It has been continuous and steadily getting worse ever since it started an hour ago. There hasn't been a single moment of relief.
Moving my head or coughing makes the pressure inside my head so much worse. Nothing I have tried gives me any relief.
No, I didn't see any flashing lights, zigzag lines, or sparkles before the headache began.
Yes, I threw up twice right before coming to the hospital, and bright room lights make the nausea worse.
No, my eyes aren't tearing up or red, and my nose isn't running or congested.
No, I haven't had any fever or chills, and my neck doesn't feel stiff.
During batting practice about three hours ago, an errant swing hit me directly on the right side of my head.
Yes, the impact knocked me out cold for about two minutes right after it happened.
When I came to, I felt totally normal and told my teammates I was fine, but about two hours later everything suddenly went downhill.
Yes, my left arm and left leg feel heavy and clumsy, and I can barely lift them.
I feel like it's taking a lot of effort to get my words out, but I haven't had any convulsions or shaking spells.
My vision has become blurry, and when I try to look around, things look doubled.
I feel extremely sleepy and foggy, and it's getting harder and harder to keep my eyes open.
I swallowed two Tylenol pills when the headache first started, but they didn't help at all.
It was solely caused by being struck with the bat, not by stress, lack of sleep, or anything I ate.
I have never had high blood pressure, and I do not take aspirin, warfarin, or any other blood thinners.
No one else is sick or has a headache, and I haven't been around any gas heaters, generators, or fumes.
No, I have never had cancer, HIV, or any problems with my immune system.
I thought it was just a typical sports concussion from the bat, but my head feels like it's going to split open.

I'm terrified that my skull is fractured and bleeding inside my head because I can't stop throwing up. I need an urgent head scan right now and something strong through an IV to stop this vomiting and pain.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with any medical conditions.
I have never had surgery, and this is the first time I've ever been admitted to an emergency room.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary supplements.
No, I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on a weekend, and I haven't had any alcohol today.
I am a twenty-two-year-old college student on the university club baseball team, living in a dormitory on campus.
There is no family history of aneurysms, strokes, early heart disease, or recurring severe headaches.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg, heart rate is 55 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, body temperature is 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
Lethargic young male appearing acutely ill, with a localized contusion and soft tissue swelling over the right temple.
Glasgow Coma Scale score is 9 with eye opening to pain (E2), confused vocal responses (V3), and motor withdrawal to painful stimuli (M4).
Right pupil is 6 mm, dilated and sluggishly reactive to light, while the left pupil is 3 mm and briskly reactive.
Right pupil dilation with sluggish light response consistent with partial right third cranial nerve palsy, without gross facial asymmetry.
Left-sided hemiparesis is present with motor strength 3/5 in the left upper and lower extremities, compared to 5/5 on the right.
Deep tendon reflexes are brisk (3+) on the left with a positive Babinski sign, and normal (2+) on the right with a flexor plantar response.
Sensory responsiveness to tactile and noxious stimuli is diminished across the left hemibody compared to the right.
The neck is supple with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Tympanic membranes are clear bilaterally with no hemotympanum, cerebrospinal fluid otorrhea, or retroauricular ecchymosis.
